## Buying a home in the United States: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes. There is no federal ban on foreigners buying homes, but about 30 states have added some limits, and Texas and Florida restrict buyers from certain countries such as China.

Costs on top of the price
2-5% · Closing costs vary by state and typically run 2-5% of the loan amount, covering title search and title insurance, recording fees, attorney fees, appraisal and lender fees; since August 2024 the seller no longer has to pay the buyer's agent, so the buyer may pay it unless the seller agrees to; FIRPTA does not apply when you buy but does when a foreigner later sells, with the buyer generally withholding 15% of the sale price.

Yearly property tax
Property tax is set locally and in 2024 averaged about 1.22% of value across the largest city in each state, from 0.30% in Honolulu to 3.02% in Detroit.

Tax on rental income
By default a non-resident pays 30% of gross rent (or a lower treaty rate), withheld at source, or can elect to treat the rent as business income and pay graduated rates on net income by filing Form 1040-NR and giving Form W-8ECI to the withholding agent.

## Buying a home in Vietnam: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Only buildings (mostly condos) on a 50-year renewable term, never land; caps of 30% of units per apartment building and 250 houses per ward.

Costs on top of the price
2.5-3.1% · New developer apartment: 10% VAT usually already in the price + 0.5% registration fee + 2% maintenance fund + notary/admin; GPG lists 2.55-3.1% buyer costs.

Yearly property tax
Non-agricultural land-use tax 0.03-0.15% of state land value; negligible for apartments.

Tax on rental income
10% of gross rent (5% VAT + 5% PIT) above the exemption threshold; threshold raised to VND 1 billion/yr from 1 Jan 2026 (older guides say VND 100 million).

What holiday rentals earn
No sourced STR gross yield found.

Long-term rent yield
3.5-4.2 (GPG Q3 2025: HCMC 4.16, Hanoi 3.54)% gross

Holiday-rental rules
Guests must be registered with local police; HCMC (Decision 19/2026, from 25 Apr 2026) allows apartment short-lets only as registered, licensed accommodation providers; frequent/multi-unit renting needs a business registration.

## How to buy a home in Bulgaria as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Yes, buildings and apartments, with rights similar to locals; per GPG, foreigners can't own land directly, so a Bulgarian company is the usual route.

### The steps

- Check what you can own: Non-EU citizens can buy apartments and buildings in their own name but not land. To buy a house with its plot, a non-EU buyer usually sets up a Bulgarian company.
- Hire a lawyer and check the property: A lawyer checks the title and debts, which usually takes 5 to 10 business days.
- Sign a preliminary contract: Pay a deposit, usually 10%. If you pull out you lose it, and if the seller pulls out they owe you double.
- Get your documents ready: You need your passport and a Bulgarian personal tax number from the National Revenue Agency. Payments of EUR 5,113 or more must go by bank transfer.
- Sign the deed before a notary: Sign the notarial deed before a notary in the property's district, with a sworn translator if you do not speak Bulgarian. The notary files it with the Registry Agency, usually in 1 to 3 business days.
- Declare the property to the municipality: File a tax declaration with the local municipality within 2 months of buying, and move the utility accounts into your name.

### Costs on top of the price

About 3.2-8.5%: Transfer tax 0.1-3% (municipal; Sofia 2.5%) + notary 0.1-1.5% + legal 0.5-1% + agent 2.5-3%.

### Every year

Yearly costs are low: municipal property tax is 0.01% to 0.45% of the tax assessment value, with a 5% discount if paid in full by April 30, plus a municipal waste collection fee. Owning through a company adds about EUR 500 to 1,500 a year in running costs.

Yearly property tax: 0.01-0.45% of the property's tax value plus a municipal garbage fee.

Tax on rental income: Non-residents: 10% final tax on gross rent, paid quarterly, no deductions.

Buying guide

## For Americans: what to report to the IRS when you own a home or an account abroad

A home abroad that you hold directly is not reportable on the FBAR or on Form 8938, according to the IRS. The foreign bank account you open for it is another matter: the FBAR applies when your foreign accounts together exceed $10,000 at any time in the year. Rent from the house is part of your worldwide income, which US citizens report wherever they live.

Reviewed on 14 November 2026 · Rules and figures as of November 2026 · General information, not legal or tax advice

### The house

The IRS comparison table of the two forms has a row for it. Foreign real estate held directly: not reportable on Form 8938, not reportable on the FBAR. Foreign real estate held through a foreign entity: the real estate is still not reported, but the entity itself is a specified foreign financial asset and its maximum value includes the value of the real estate. Buying through a company abroad therefore changes your reporting.

Source: [Internal Revenue Service](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements)

### The bank account that comes with it

- FBAR: required when the aggregate value of your foreign financial accounts exceeds $10,000 at any time during the calendar year. It is a cumulative balance, so two accounts that together pass $10,000 are both reported. It is filed electronically with FinCEN, not with your tax return.
- Form 8938, living in the US: total foreign financial assets above $50,000 on the last day of the tax year or $75,000 at any time for an unmarried filer; $100,000 and $150,000 for a married couple filing jointly.
- Form 8938, living abroad: above $200,000 on the last day or $300,000 at any time for an unmarried filer; $400,000 and $600,000 for a married couple filing jointly.

The moment to watch is the purchase itself: if you move the price through an account in your name abroad, that account passes $10,000 on that day even if it is empty a week later.

Source: [Internal Revenue Service](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements)

### Rent and a later sale

US citizens and resident aliens are taxed on worldwide income from all sources, the IRS says, whether they are in the United States or abroad. Rent from a house in Italy belongs in the US return as well as in the Italian one; the foreign tax credit exists so that the same income is not fully taxed twice, and it has to be claimed. See [Do I pay tax in my own country too?](https://realhunt.co/guide/questions/do-i-pay-tax-at-home-too).

Source: [Internal Revenue Service](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/us-citizens-and-resident-aliens-abroad)

Buying guide

## Opening a bank account and paying for a home in another country

If you live legally in an EU country, a bank in any EU country cannot refuse you a basic payment account just because you live elsewhere. Outside that right, each bank decides. Spain, Sweden and the Netherlands in practice expect a local account or one that can pay the notary on time; the price itself almost always travels by bank transfer to the notary or the seller, never in cash.

Reviewed on 14 November 2026 · Rules and figures as of November 2026 · General information, not legal or tax advice

### The EU right to a basic account

The EU's own guide says that anyone legally resident in an EU country is entitled to open a basic payment account, and that banks cannot refuse an application just because the person does not live in the country where the bank is established. The right covers a basic account only, not savings accounts.

A bank can still refuse if you do not meet the rules against money laundering, and in some countries if you already hold a similar account there. Applying from another country, you may be asked to prove a genuine interest, and buying a home is one. Before opening, the bank must give you a fee information document.

This right belongs to EU residents. A buyer who lives in the United Kingdom, the United States or elsewhere depends on each bank's own policy; we have no official list of the papers each bank asks for, so we do not print one.

Source: [Your Europe (European Union)](https://europa.eu/youreurope/citizens/consumers/financial-products-and-services/bank-accounts-eu/index_en.htm)

### Where a local account is expected

- Spain: most notaries and town halls expect payments and bills to go through a Spanish account.
- Sweden: a Swedish account is normally needed to complete the payment.
- The Netherlands: you need an account that can pay the notary on time.
- Denmark: Danish banks usually lend up to 80% of the value, so plan for at least a 20% down payment.

Sources: [RealHunt country file: Spain](https://realhunt.co/costs/spain) · [RealHunt country file: Sweden](https://realhunt.co/costs/sweden) · [RealHunt country file: Netherlands](https://realhunt.co/costs/netherlands) · [RealHunt country file: Denmark](https://realhunt.co/costs/denmark)

### How the price is paid

- France: the balance and the fees go to the notary's account before the day of the deed; the deposit sits in the notary's blocked account until then.
- The Netherlands: the usual 10% deposit, or a bank guarantee, is paid to the notary.
- Bulgaria: payments of EUR 5,113 or more must go by bank transfer.
- Japan: non-residents usually pay in full, since Japanese banks rarely lend to them, and must report the purchase to the Bank of Japan within 20 days.

Inside the EU, a bank must charge the same for a payment in euros to another EU country as for a domestic one. That rule is about fees in euros; it says nothing about the exchange rate when your money is in pounds, dollars or kronor. We have no sourced comparison of banks and currency brokers, so we make none: ask for the total you will receive in the seller's currency, in writing, from each.

Sources: [RealHunt country file: France](https://realhunt.co/costs/france) · [RealHunt country file: Netherlands](https://realhunt.co/costs/netherlands) · [RealHunt country file: Bulgaria](https://realhunt.co/costs/bulgaria) · [RealHunt country file: Japan](https://realhunt.co/costs/japan) · [Your Europe (European Union)](https://europa.eu/youreurope/citizens/consumers/financial-products-and-services/payments-transfers-cheques/index_en.htm)

Buying guide

## Buying a home in Europe with a British passport after Brexit

Brexit did not stop British citizens buying homes in the EU: in most countries they buy on the same terms as before. What changed is everything around the house. Without a visa you can spend 90 days in every 180 in the whole Schengen area, you are taxed as a non-EU owner and your pet needs a new certificate for every trip.

Reviewed on 14 November 2026 · Rules and figures as of November 2026 · General information, not legal or tax advice

### How long you can stay in your house

The UK government's travel guidance is plain: you do not need a visa for short trips if you stay 90 days or less in a 180-day period, and your total stay in the Schengen area must be no more than 90 days in every 180. It does not matter how many countries you visit, and the 180-day period keeps rolling. The guidance makes no exception for people who own a home there.

In practice: a summer from 1 June to 29 August uses all 90 days. You cannot come back for the October half-term, because looking back 180 days from then you would still be over the limit. To live in the house for longer you need a visa or a residence permit from that country: see [visas and residency](https://realhunt.co/guide/buying/visas-and-residency).

Source: [GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/travel-to-eu-schengen-area)

### Taxed as a non-EU owner

Since Brexit, British buyers count as non-EU buyers, so the non-EU rules and rates apply. Two examples from our country files: in Spain a non-resident from the EU pays 19% on net rental income, while a non-EU owner pays 24% on the gross rent with no deductions; in France the 7.5% social charge applies to people covered by social security in another EU or EEA country or Switzerland, and others pay 17.2%.

At home, a UK resident normally pays UK tax on foreign income, and the government's list of such income includes rental income on overseas property. If the same income is taxed in both countries, you can usually claim relief.

Sources: [RealHunt rules by nationality](https://realhunt.co/can-i-buy) · [RealHunt country file: Spain](https://realhunt.co/costs/spain) · [RealHunt country file: France](https://realhunt.co/costs/france) · [GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/tax-foreign-income) · [GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/tax-foreign-income/taxed-twice)

### Pets

A pet passport issued in Great Britain is no longer valid for the EU. Your dog, cat or ferret needs an animal health certificate from a vet for each trip, valid for 10 days for entry into the EU. More in [moving with pets](https://realhunt.co/guide/buying/moving-with-pets).

Source: [GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/taking-your-pet-abroad)

Buying guide

## Buying a house together when you are not married, or between friends

The law of the country where the house stands decides how co-owners hold it, not your relationship. In England you choose between two forms with opposite results on death. In Spain shares are presumed equal unless you write otherwise, and any co-owner can ask to divide the property at any time. Write the shares, and what happens if one of you wants out, into the deed.

Reviewed on 14 November 2026 · Rules and figures as of November 2026 · General information, not legal or tax advice

### England and Wales: joint tenants or tenants in common

You must decide which type of joint ownership you want when you buy, and tell HM Land Registry when you register the property.

- As joint tenants you have equal rights to the whole property, it automatically goes to the other owners if you die, and you cannot pass on your ownership in your will.
- As tenants in common you can own different shares, your share does not automatically go to the others if you die, and you can pass it on in your will.

Two friends who put in 70% and 30% want the second form. You can change from one to the other later, for example after a separation, and there is no fee.

Source: [GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/joint-property-ownership)

### Spain: proindiviso

The Civil Code calls it community of property: a thing belongs pro indiviso to several people. Benefits and costs are shared in proportion to each owner's share, and the shares are presumed equal unless the contrary is proved (article 393). If one of you pays more, say so in the deed.

Article 400 is the one to know before buying with friends: no co-owner is obliged to stay in the community, and each can ask at any time for the common thing to be divided. An agreement to keep it undivided is valid for a set time of no more than ten years, and can be renewed.

Source: [Boletín Oficial del Estado](https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1889-4763)

### France: indivision, and buying from several heirs

In France, property held by several people without separate parts is in indivision. The clearest official description is for inheritances: when someone dies leaving several heirs, the property belongs to all of them together. They can sign an agreement to organise it, for a fixed term of up to five years, renewable, or for an indefinite time, and can name a manager.

A co-owner can sell their own rights, but if the buyer is an outsider they must first notify the other co-owners through a court officer. For you as a buyer this means one thing: when a cheap house is sold by brothers and sisters, ask the notary at the start to confirm who the owners are and that every one of them is a party to the sale. A house where one heir cannot be found is not ready to be sold.

Source: [Service-Public.gouv.fr](https://www.service-public.gouv.fr/particuliers/vosdroits/F1296)

Buying guide

## Buying a house at a court auction in Spain and Germany: deposit, minimum bid and what you take on

A court auction can be cheaper than the market, and it moves the risk to you. In Spain a bidder first deposits 20% of the valuation and, by bidding, accepts the title as it stands and the charges that rank before the debt being enforced. In Germany the security is one tenth of the market value set by the court, and a first-round bid under half that value is refused. You bid without the checks of a normal purchase.

Reviewed on 14 November 2026 · Rules and figures as of November 2026 · General information, not legal or tax advice

### Spain

Court auctions are held on the electronic auctions portal of the state gazette agency, where properties can be searched by province.

- The deposit: to take part, article 669 of the Civil Procedure Act requires bidders to deposit first an amount equal to 20% of the value given to the property, with a minimum of €1,000. The court officer in charge may raise or lower that percentage.
- What you accept by bidding: the same article says that, by the mere fact of taking part, bidders accept as sufficient the title documents in the court file, or that there are none, and accept to take over the charges that rank before the debt being enforced if the property is awarded to them. An earlier mortgage does not disappear: it becomes yours.
- What the file holds: under article 656 the registrar sends the court a certificate of who owns the property and the complete list of the charges registered on it. Read it before bidding.
- When the bid is approved: if the best bid is 70% or more of the value at which the property went to auction, it is approved the day after the auction closes, and the winner has twenty days to pay the difference between the deposit and the price (article 670).

Sources: [Agencia Estatal Boletín Oficial del Estado](https://subastas.boe.es/) · [Boletín Oficial del Estado](https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2000-323)

### Germany

- The value: the enforcement court sets the market value of the property (Verkehrswert), if necessary after hearing experts.
- The security: under section 68 of the Forced Sale Act it is one tenth of that value.
- The floor: under section 85a the award must be refused if the highest bid, counting the rights that stay on the property, does not reach half of the property's value. A new date is then set, and at that second date the award can no longer be refused for this reason.
- The wait: when an award is refused, the time between the two dates should be at least three months and may not exceed six.

Sources: [Bundesministerium der Justiz](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/zvg/__68.html) · [Bundesministerium der Justiz](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/zvg/__85a.html) · [Bundesministerium der Justiz](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/zvg/__74a.html)

### What a normal purchase gives you and an auction does not

In a normal purchase you visit the house, the seller answers for what they told you and a notary checks the title. At auction you may not get inside, nobody answers for the state of the building, and in Spain you take the title as it is. We have only read the Spanish and German rules; for Italy, France and Portugal we have no sourced summary yet, so we give none. If you bid, have a local lawyer read the court file first: see [do I need a lawyer?](https://realhunt.co/guide/questions/do-i-need-a-lawyer).

Buying guide

## After the purchase: what a home abroad costs every year, in 20 countries

The yearly bill has three parts: the local property tax, the running costs of any house, and a few costs that only an owner from abroad meets, such as a tax representative in Japan, a bank trust fee in Mexico or a company in Bulgaria. The property tax ranges from a fixed fee in Sweden to about 1% of the value, on average, in large US cities.

Reviewed on 14 November 2026 · Rules and figures as of November 2026 · General information, not legal or tax advice

### Yearly property tax and other yearly costs, country by country

From our country files; the sources of each row are on the country's costs page, linked in the first column.

Country | Yearly property tax | Also every year
[Bulgaria](https://realhunt.co/costs/bulgaria) | 0.01-0.45% of the property's tax value plus a municipal garbage fee. | Yearly costs are low: municipal property tax is 0.01% to 0.45% of the tax assessment value, with a 5% discount if paid in full by April 30, plus a municipal waste collection fee. Owning through a company adds about EUR 500 to 1,500 a year in running costs.
[Canada](https://realhunt.co/costs/canada) | Property tax is set by each city as a share of assessed value, from about 0.3% in Vancouver to 2.12% in Saint John in 2026. | Expect municipal property tax, from about 0.3% to 2.1% of assessed value depending on the city, plus insurance and upkeep. The federal Underused Housing Tax is proposed to end from 2025, but the change was still in Bill C-15 when last checked.
[Cyprus](https://realhunt.co/costs/cyprus) | There is no annual national property tax (abolished in 2017); owners pay municipal fees of about €90 to €300 a year, plus sewerage and local authority charges. | Yearly costs are municipal, sewerage and local authority fees, plus income tax and GHS on any rent.
[Denmark](https://realhunt.co/costs/denmark) | Owners pay property value tax (ejendomsværdiskat) of 0.51% on 80% of the official valuation (1.4% above DKK 9.2 million) plus municipal land tax (grundskyld) at a rate set by each municipality, capped at 30 per mille of the land value. | Expect property value tax and municipal land tax, both charged through the Danish tax system, plus insurance, utilities and upkeep. Owners abroad may need to file a Danish tax return if they rent the home out.
[Dominican Republic](https://realhunt.co/costs/dominican-republic) | The yearly IPI tax is 1% of the part of a person's total Dominican property value, as assessed by the tax office DGII, above RD$10,695,494 in 2026, so a single cheap home is often below the threshold. | Most single homes under about $150,000 pay no IPI property tax because they fall under the threshold, but expect condo fees, utilities and upkeep. A 2026 tax law (Law 30-26) sets a 10% tax on gains when an individual sells, though its regulations were still in draft in October 2026.
[France](https://realhunt.co/costs/france) | Owners pay an annual property tax (taxe foncière) set by the local authorities, and owners of a furnished second home also pay housing tax (taxe d'habitation), which some communes raise by a surcharge of 5% to 60%. | Expect the annual taxe foncière, plus taxe d'habitation if the home is a furnished second home, and income tax and social charges on any rent.
[Germany](https://realhunt.co/costs/germany) | Owners pay property tax (Grundsteuer), calculated since 2025 as assessed value x a tax rate x a municipal multiplier (Hebesatz) that each municipality sets. | Expect the municipal property tax, insurance, utilities and upkeep. Rental profit is taxable in Germany, so a non-resident landlord deals with a German tax office.
[Greece](https://realhunt.co/costs/greece) | Owners on 1 January pay the unified property tax (ENFIA), calculated per property from its location, size, age and official zone value, with an extra charge if total Greek property exceeds €500,000. | Yearly costs are ENFIA and income tax on any rent.
[Italy](https://realhunt.co/costs/italy) | IMU 0.4-1.06% on second homes (on cadastral value). | IMU (council property tax) on second homes and a local waste tax (TARI). For small rural houses these are often a few hundred euros a year.
[Japan](https://realhunt.co/costs/japan) | Fixed asset tax is 1.4% of the government's assessed value, plus city planning tax of up to 0.3% in urban areas, and small residential plots get a lower tax base. | Expect fixed asset tax of 1.4% and city planning tax of up to 0.3% of assessed value, which is usually well below market value. Add the cost of a tax representative and, for apartments, monthly management and repair fund fees.
[Mexico](https://realhunt.co/costs/mexico) | Municipal predial, set locally on cadastral value; usually small, often less than HOA fees. | Yearly costs include the local property tax (predial), usually 0.05% to 1.2% of the official cadastral value, which is often well below market value. In the restricted zone add the bank trust fee, about US$450 to US$1,000 a year, plus HOA fees, insurance and upkeep.
[Netherlands](https://realhunt.co/costs/netherlands) | Owners pay municipal property tax (onroerendezaakbelasting, OZB) on the official WOZ value, at a rate each municipality sets, which in practice is a per mille figure; tenants of homes do not pay it. | Expect municipal property tax (OZB), insurance and upkeep, and in a flat the owners' association (VvE) contribution. Non-residents also pay box 3 income tax based on the property's value.
[Norway](https://realhunt.co/costs/norway) | Some municipalities charge property tax (eiendomsskatt), at most 4 per mille of the value after a reduction of at least 30%, and some also give a basic deduction; many charge nothing. | Expect municipal property tax where it applies, municipal fees, insurance and upkeep. Costs such as municipal fees and property tax are deductible against rental income.
[Poland](https://realhunt.co/costs/poland) | Owners pay a local property tax (podatek od nieruchomości) set by the commune, capped in 2026 at PLN 1.25 per m² of usable floor space for flats and houses. | Yearly costs are the local property tax, which is low for flats, plus income tax on any rent.
[Portugal](https://realhunt.co/costs/portugal) | IMI 0.3-0.45% of taxable value (urban), set by municipality. | IMI (council tax), usually 0.3–0.45% of the tax value for urban property.
[Spain](https://realhunt.co/costs/spain) | IBI 0.4-1.1% of cadastral value (municipal), plus imputed income tax on unlet homes. | IBI (council tax) and waste collection. Non-residents who do not rent the house out also file a small yearly imputed-income tax.
[Sweden](https://realhunt.co/costs/sweden) | Houses pay a municipal property fee (kommunal fastighetsavgift) of SEK 10,425 in 2026, or 0.75% of the tax value if that is lower. | House owners pay the municipal property fee and must file a Swedish tax return if they owe it or have rental income, even when living abroad. Add insurance, utilities and upkeep.
[Switzerland](https://realhunt.co/costs/switzerland) | More than half of the cantons charge an annual property tax (Liegenschaftssteuer), usually 0.01-0.3% of the assessed value, and owners also pay cantonal wealth tax on the property value minus the mortgage. | Yearly costs are wealth tax, cantonal property tax where it exists, and tax on imputed rental value (Eigenmietwert) if you use the home yourself. Imputed rental value is due to end on 1 January 2029, and cantons may then add a new tax on second homes.
[United Kingdom](https://realhunt.co/costs/united-kingdom) | Owners or occupiers pay council tax to the local council, and many councils in England charge second homes a premium of up to 100% from April 2025. | Yearly costs are council tax, which may include a second home premium, plus a self assessment tax return and income tax if you let the home.
[United States](https://realhunt.co/costs/united-states) | Property tax is set locally and in 2024 averaged about 1.22% of value across the largest city in each state, from 0.30% in Honolulu to 3.02% in Detroit. | Expect local property tax, which is often around 1% of value but varies widely by city, plus insurance and upkeep. If you rent it out you also file a US tax return each year when you use the net-income election.

### Costs that only an owner from abroad has

- Japan: a tax representative with a Japanese address to receive and pay the tax bills, and for flats the monthly management and repair fund fees.
- Mexico: in the restricted zone, the bank trust fee of about US$450 to US$1,000 a year.
- Bulgaria: owning through a company, as buyers from outside the EU do for a house with land, adds about EUR 500 to 1,500 a year.
- Spain: a non-resident who does not let the house declares imputed income on it each year.
- The Netherlands: non-residents pay box 3 income tax based on the value of the property.
- France: a furnished second home also pays housing tax, which some communes raise by 5% to 60%.

Sources: [RealHunt country file: Japan](https://realhunt.co/costs/japan) · [RealHunt country file: Mexico](https://realhunt.co/costs/mexico) · [RealHunt country file: Bulgaria](https://realhunt.co/costs/bulgaria) · [Agencia Tributaria](https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/no-residentes/irnr-sin-establecimiento-permanente/cuestiones-especificas-sobre-tributacion-inmuebles.html) · [RealHunt country file: Netherlands](https://realhunt.co/costs/netherlands) · [RealHunt country file: France](https://realhunt.co/costs/france)

### The first twelve months

Some jobs come once, in the first weeks: in Bulgaria you file a tax declaration with the municipality within two months of buying and move the utility accounts into your name; in Japan you report the purchase to the Bank of Japan within 20 days; in Spain bills are expected to go through a Spanish account.

We have no sourced figures for furniture, travel, insurance for a house that stands empty or a neighbour who keeps the keys, so we print none. On each home we list we show the community fees and the yearly tax whenever the listing states them.

Buying guide

## Who inspects the house before you buy it, country by country

It depends on who the country makes responsible. France obliges the seller to give you a file of technical surveys. In the Netherlands, Sweden, Germany and the United States no report comes with the house: an inspection is something the buyer orders and pays for. In Denmark the buyer's lawyer reviews a condition report before the contract becomes final.

Reviewed on 14 November 2026 · Rules and figures as of November 2026 · General information, not legal or tax advice

### France: the seller pays for a file of surveys

The seller must give the buyer the dossier de diagnostic technique with the preliminary contract or the deed. What goes in it depends on the house:

- the energy rating (DPE), and an energy audit if a house is rated E, F or G;
- a lead report if it was built before 1 January 1949;
- an asbestos report if the building permit is from before 1 July 1997;
- reports on the electricity and gas installations when they are more than 15 years old;
- a report on the septic system when the house is not on mains drainage, which is common in the countryside;
- a termite report in areas declared infested by the prefect.

The contract must also say whether the area carries a risk of dry rot (mérule). None of this is a structural survey: it tells you about specific risks, not about the roof.

Source: [Service-Public.gouv.fr](https://www.service-public.gouv.fr/particuliers/vosdroits/F10798)

### The Netherlands, Sweden, Germany and the United States: the buyer decides

- The Netherlands: the government lists the building survey (bouwkundige keuring) among the buyer's possible costs, next to the agent and the valuation. It is optional.
- Sweden: our guide says to visit the property and consider hiring an inspector before signing. Remember that bids bind nobody until the contract is signed, so there is time.
- Germany: the notary is neutral and does not act for you, so our guide suggests your own lawyer and a survey.
- United States: the consumer bureau describes the home inspection as often part of the buying process; our guide pairs it with a title search before closing.

Sources: [Rijksoverheid](https://www.rijksoverheid.nl/documenten/vraag-en-antwoord/huis-kopen/met-welke-kosten-krijg-ik-te-maken-als-ik-een-huis-koop) · [RealHunt country file: Sweden](https://realhunt.co/costs/sweden) · [RealHunt country file: Germany](https://realhunt.co/costs/germany) · [Consumer Financial Protection Bureau](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/mortgages/answers/key-terms/) · [RealHunt country file: United States](https://realhunt.co/costs/united-states)

### Denmark, Italy and Spain: papers to read rather than a survey to order

- Denmark: your lawyer reviews the condition report, the title and the registered charges before the bank and lawyer approval clauses are lifted.
- Italy: ask for proof that the building matches its plans and for the energy certificate.
- Spain: in the countryside, check the status of the land and that every building is legal.

We have no sourced figure for what an inspection costs in each country, so we give none. Ask two local inspectors for a written quote before the viewing trip. Our [viewing checklist](https://realhunt.co/blog/viewing-checklist-cheap-house) lists what to look at yourself.

Sources: [RealHunt country file: Denmark](https://realhunt.co/costs/denmark) · [RealHunt country file: Italy](https://realhunt.co/costs/italy) · [RealHunt country file: Spain](https://realhunt.co/costs/spain)

Buying guide

## What happens to your home in another country when you die: the EU rules

In the EU, your whole inheritance, including a house in another country, is normally handled by the authority of the EU country where you last lived, under that country's law. You can choose the law of your nationality instead, but you have to say so clearly in a will. Denmark and Ireland do not apply these rules, and inheritance tax is a separate matter in each country.

Reviewed on 14 November 2026 · Rules and figures as of November 2026 · General information, not legal or tax advice

### One law for everything you own

The EU's guide for citizens explains that an inheritance is usually handled by an authority, often a court or a notary, in the EU country where the person last lived, and that this authority will in most cases apply its own national law. That law governs all the assets, wherever they are and whether they are movable, like a car or a bank account, or immovable, like a house.

So if you retire to your house in Portugal and die living there, Portuguese law decides who inherits your Portuguese house and also what you left in your home country, unless you chose otherwise.

Source: [Your Europe (European Union)](https://europa.eu/youreurope/citizens/family/inheritances/planning-inheritance/index_en.htm)

### Choosing the law of your nationality

EU rules let you choose that the law of your country of nationality applies, whether or not that country is in the EU. With several nationalities you can choose any of them. The choice has to be made explicitly and clearly, in a will or a separate declaration.

This is the point for an owner from outside the EU: a British or American owner of a house in Spain or Italy can choose their own national law in a will. The authority handling the inheritance can refuse to apply particular provisions of that law in some cases, so a will for a house abroad is a job for a notary or lawyer who knows both systems.

Source: [Your Europe (European Union)](https://europa.eu/youreurope/citizens/family/inheritances/planning-inheritance/index_en.htm)

### Where the rules stop

The EU rules on inheritance do not apply in Denmark and Ireland. If the heirs settle the inheritance with an authority there, your choice of law may not be taken into account. Danish and Irish citizens can still use the rules, and choose their national law, when the inheritance is handled in another EU country.

These rules decide who inherits and how. They do not set the tax: inheritance tax depends on each country and sometimes on each region, and we have no sourced table of it, so we give none. For a house outside the EU, such as Japan, Mexico or the United States, the law of that country applies and you should ask there.

Source: [Your Europe (European Union)](https://europa.eu/youreurope/citizens/family/inheritances/planning-inheritance/index_en.htm)

Buying guide

## Taking a dog, cat or ferret to your home in another country

For the EU the order is: microchip, rabies vaccination, then the travel document. Between EU countries that document is the European pet passport, which only owners resident in the EU can get. From Great Britain and other non-EU countries it is an animal health certificate, issued by a vet for each trip. Dogs going to Finland, Ireland, Malta, Norway or Northern Ireland also need tapeworm treatment.

Reviewed on 14 November 2026 · Rules and figures as of November 2026 · General information, not legal or tax advice

### Into and between EU countries

The EU's guide lists what a dog, cat or ferret needs to travel with you to another EU country, or from outside the EU into it:

- a microchip (or a clearly readable tattoo applied before 3 July 2011);
- vaccination against rabies;
- a rabies antibody test when that is required for the non-EU country you are travelling from;
- treatment against the tapeworm Echinococcus multilocularis when the destination is free from it: Finland, Ireland, Malta, Norway and Northern Ireland;
- a valid European pet passport when travelling between EU countries, or an EU animal health certificate when coming from a non-EU country.

The European pet passport is issued only to owners who are resident in the EU, by any authorised vet. You can travel with up to five pets; more than five needs proof that they are going to a competition, show or sporting event.

Source: [Your Europe (European Union)](https://europa.eu/youreurope/citizens/travel/carry/animal-plant/index_en.htm)

### From Great Britain

The UK government sets out the steps for a trip to the EU. Microchip your pet before, or at the same time as, the rabies vaccination; otherwise it has to be vaccinated again. Then get an animal health certificate from your vet. It is valid for 10 days for entry into the EU, for 6 months for onward travel inside the EU and for 6 months for re-entry to Great Britain, and you need a new one for each trip.

If you live in England, Scotland or Wales you cannot use a pet passport to enter the EU, even one that was issued in the EU. For an owner who goes to the house three times a year that means three certificates a year, so ask your vet for the price before you plan the trips.

Source: [GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/taking-your-pet-abroad)

### Other countries

We have only read the EU and UK rules. Japan, the United States, Mexico and other countries outside the EU have their own, which can include waiting periods, and we have not sourced them, so we do not describe them. Ask the agriculture or animal health authority of the country before you book.

Buying guide

## Buying from a distance: power of attorney, who signs and what still needs you

Yes, in several countries the deed can be signed by someone holding your power of attorney: our files say so for Italy, France, Germany and Greece. A power signed in your own country normally needs an apostille to be accepted in another. Tax numbers can often be obtained at a consulate or through a representative, and in Japan the legal explanation can be given by video call.

Reviewed on 14 November 2026 · Rules and figures as of November 2026 · General information, not legal or tax advice

### Where a power of attorney is used

- Italy: the deed (rogito) is signed before a notary, and you can sign by power of attorney if you cannot travel.
- France: you sign the final deed in person or by power of attorney, after sending the balance and the fees to the notary's account.
- Germany: both sides sign in front of the notary, and you can sign through a certified power of attorney from abroad.
- Greece: a lawyer can act for you under a power of attorney, from the title check to the deed.

Sources: [RealHunt country file: Italy](https://realhunt.co/costs/italy) · [RealHunt country file: France](https://realhunt.co/costs/france) · [RealHunt country file: Germany](https://realhunt.co/costs/germany) · [RealHunt country file: Greece](https://realhunt.co/costs/greece)

### Making a document from home valid abroad: the apostille

A power of attorney signed before a notary in your country is a public document of that country. The 1961 Apostille Convention replaces the old chain of legalisations with a single certificate, the apostille, issued by a competent authority in the place where the document originates. The Hague Conference counts 130 contracting parties.

An electronic apostille is as valid as a paper one and must be accepted by all contracting parties. Ask the notary abroad for the exact wording they need before you sign anything at home: a power that does not name the property or the powers clearly may be refused.

Source: [Hague Conference on Private International Law](https://www.hcch.net/en/instruments/conventions/specialised-sections/apostille)

### What else can be done without travelling

- Tax numbers: the Spanish NIE can be requested at a Spanish consulate, the Italian codice fiscale at an Italian consulate, and the Portuguese NIF through a representative.
- Japan: the explanation of the property's legal status that must come before the contract can be done by video call.
- Money: in Mexico our guide says not to wire a deposit until the documents and the title have been reviewed. That is sound anywhere.

What nobody can do for you from a distance is see the house. If you cannot go, have someone you pay, and who does not earn from the sale, visit it. We have no sourced figures for what a power of attorney costs in each country, so we give none.

Sources: [RealHunt country file: Spain](https://realhunt.co/costs/spain) · [RealHunt country file: Italy](https://realhunt.co/costs/italy) · [RealHunt country file: Portugal](https://realhunt.co/costs/portugal) · [RealHunt country file: Japan](https://realhunt.co/costs/japan) · [RealHunt country file: Mexico](https://realhunt.co/costs/mexico)

Buying guide

## The papers that prove who owns a house and what it owes, country by country

Every country keeps a public record of who owns a property and which debts sit on it, and in most of them you can read it before you pay anything. In Spain, Italy, Portugal and England a buyer can get the extract directly; in Germany you need to show a legitimate interest. Ask for it before the deposit, not after.

Reviewed on 14 November 2026 · Rules and figures as of November 2026 · General information, not legal or tax advice

### Spain: nota simple

The nota simple is the informative extract of the Land Registry. The registrars explain that it identifies the property and names the holder or holders of the registered rights (full ownership, mortgage, usufruct) with their extent and limits. It is informative only and does not certify the entries.

You can request it online from the registrars' own site, and it can come with an English translation if you ask. Our Spain guide adds two more things to ask the seller for: the last receipts of the yearly council tax (IBI) and, in the countryside, proof of the land status and that the buildings are legal. See the [Spain glossary](https://realhunt.co/guide/glossary/spain).

Sources: [Colegio de Registradores de España](https://sede.registradores.org/site/propiedad?lang=es_ES) · [RealHunt country file: Spain](https://realhunt.co/costs/spain)

### Italy: visura catastale

The Italian tax agency states that the information in the cadastral and mortgage databases is public and that access is open to everyone. The exception is the floor plans (planimetrie), which only people with rights over the property can consult. Owners can also consult their own properties online.

The cadastral extract (visura catastale) is not the whole story. Our Italy guide asks for it together with proof that the building matches its plans (conformità urbanistica e catastale), the energy certificate (APE) and any unpaid debts. The notary checks the title before the deed. See the [Italy glossary](https://realhunt.co/guide/glossary/italy).

Sources: [Agenzia delle Entrate](https://www.agenziaentrate.gov.it/portale/schede/fabbricatiterreni/consultazione-personale/scheda-info-consultazione-personale-cittadini) · [RealHunt country file: Italy](https://realhunt.co/costs/italy)

### Portugal: certidão permanente and caderneta predial

The permanent certificate (certidão permanente) is the land registry record of the property, kept online. The justice portal says it is valid for six months, is always up to date and has to be shown when a property is bought or sold. It names the owner and the registered debts.

The caderneta predial is the tax office's record: tax value and whether the property is urban or rustic. Ask for both and for the habitation licence (licença de utilização). See the [Portugal glossary](https://realhunt.co/guide/glossary/portugal).

Sources: [Justiça.gov.pt](https://justica.gov.pt/Servicos/Pedir-certidao-permanente-de-registo-predial) · [RealHunt country file: Portugal](https://realhunt.co/costs/portugal)

### Germany: Grundbuch

The German land register is not open to the curious. Section 12 of the Land Register Code allows inspection to anyone who shows a legitimate interest. In a purchase the notary works with the register: after the contract the notary enters a priority notice (Vormerkung) that protects the buyer against other sales, and the register enters the buyer as owner once the transfer tax is paid. See the [Germany glossary](https://realhunt.co/guide/glossary/germany).

Sources: [Bundesministerium der Justiz](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/gbo/__12.html) · [Bundesministerium der Justiz](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/bgb/__883.html) · [RealHunt country file: Germany](https://realhunt.co/costs/germany)

### England and Wales: title register

HM Land Registry lets anyone search a property online. The property summary is free. The title register and the title plan cost £7 each to download; official copies sent by post cost £11 per document. The title register usually includes the title number, who owns the property, how much it last sold for and whether it has a mortgage. The title plan shows the location and the general boundaries.

Source: [GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/search-property-information-land-registry)

### France, the Netherlands, Greece, Japan and the United States

- France: the notary checks ownership, boundaries and rights of way, and the seller must attach the file of compulsory surveys to the preliminary contract or the deed.
- The Netherlands: you become the owner when the notary's transfer deed is registered with the Kadaster.
- Greece: a lawyer checks ownership and searches the land registry for mortgages, liens and claims.
- Japan: before the contract, a licensed specialist must explain the legal status of the property to the buyer, and this can be done by video call.
- United States: a title search shows that the title is clean, and the deed is recorded with the county after closing.

Sources: [RealHunt country file: France](https://realhunt.co/costs/france) · [Service-Public.gouv.fr](https://www.service-public.gouv.fr/particuliers/vosdroits/F10798) · [RealHunt country file: Netherlands](https://realhunt.co/costs/netherlands) · [RealHunt country file: Greece](https://realhunt.co/costs/greece) · [RealHunt country file: Japan](https://realhunt.co/costs/japan) · [RealHunt country file: United States](https://realhunt.co/costs/united-states)

Buying guide

## Renting out your home when you are not there: licence and tax, country by country

Before you count on any rent, check two things in the country of the house: whether a holiday let needs a licence or a registration number, and how rent paid to a non-resident is taxed. Spain, Italy and Portugal all require registration for tourist lets, and some cities have stopped giving new licences. We promise no income: the table below is about rules, not returns.

Reviewed on 14 November 2026 · Rules and figures as of November 2026 · General information, not legal or tax advice

### Spain, Italy, Portugal and Greece: the licence comes first

- Spain: a regional tourist licence plus the national single rental registry number, mandatory since 1 July 2025. New tourist lets in apartment blocks need the approval of three fifths of the owners, since 3 April 2025. Licences are regional, so the rule for a village in Granada is not the rule for Valencia: check the region before you buy.
- Italy: every tourist let needs a national identification code (CIN), shown on the listings and at the property. From the third property the activity is treated as a business.
- Portugal: registration as local lodging (Alojamento Local) is mandatory. Since November 2024 municipalities can freeze new licences in containment zones, which Lisbon and Porto use, and the owners of a building can object with more than half of the votes.
- Greece: our file has the tax scale for rent received by non-residents, but no sourced summary of the short-let rules, so we do not describe them.

Sources: [RealHunt country file: Spain](https://realhunt.co/costs/spain) · [RealHunt country file: Italy](https://realhunt.co/costs/italy) · [RealHunt country file: Portugal](https://realhunt.co/costs/portugal) · [RealHunt country file: Greece](https://realhunt.co/costs/greece)

### Tax on rent and holiday-let rules in 27 countries

From our country files. The sources behind each row are on the country's costs page, linked in the first column.

Country | Tax on rent for an owner from abroad | Holiday-let rules
[Albania](https://realhunt.co/costs/albania) | Flat 15% on rental income, including short-term, declared via the DIVA platform. | No licence or business tax ID (NIPT) required for individuals; income must be declared on DIVA, with new reporting obligations from 2026.
[Bali](https://realhunt.co/costs/bali) | Non-residents: 20% withholding on gross rent (10% possible under a tax treaty); PT PMA companies 22% corporate tax. | Short-term renting requires a Pondok Wisata (homestay) licence; foreigners cannot hold it personally and need a PT PMA with the right KBLI code plus PBG/SLF building permits.
[Bulgaria](https://realhunt.co/costs/bulgaria) | Non-residents: 10% final tax on gross rent, paid quarterly, no deductions. | Tourist accommodation must be categorised or registered with the municipality under the Tourism Act; tourist tax BGN 0.20-3.00 per night.
[Canada](https://realhunt.co/costs/canada) | Non-residents have 25% of gross rent withheld, but they can file a Section 216 return to pay tax on net rent instead, and Form NR6 lets the agent withhold on net rent. | No sourced summary
[Cyprus](https://realhunt.co/costs/cyprus) | Non-residents pay income tax on Cyprus rental income at 20% to 35% after deducting 20% of the gross rent and loan interest, plus a 2.65% health contribution (GHS); the special defence contribution does not apply to them. | No sourced summary
[Denmark](https://realhunt.co/costs/denmark) | A non-resident who rents out a Danish home is taxed in Denmark on the profit under the ordinary Danish rules; staying in Denmark more than 3 months at a time or 180 days a year, or working there, makes you fully tax liable. | No sourced summary
[Dominican Republic](https://realhunt.co/costs/dominican-republic) | Rent paid abroad to a non-resident is generally subject to 27% withholding. | No sourced summary
[France](https://realhunt.co/costs/france) | Non-residents pay French income tax on French rental income at a minimum rate of 20% (30% above about €27,500), plus social charges of 17.2%, or 7.5% for people covered by social security in another EU/EEA country or Switzerland. | No sourced summary
[Georgia](https://realhunt.co/costs/georgia) | 5% of gross rent on residential property (long- or short-term), residents and non-residents alike. | No specific short-term rental licence found in sources; the 5% rental tax applies.
[Germany](https://realhunt.co/costs/germany) | Non-resident owners are taxed in Germany on net rental income at the normal progressive income tax rates, but without the basic tax-free allowance (Grundfreibetrag). | No sourced summary
[Greece](https://realhunt.co/costs/greece) | Non-residents pay Greek tax on Greek rental income at 15% up to €12,000, 25% to €24,000, 35% to €36,000 and 45% above, after a flat 5% deduction for expenses. | No sourced summary
[Italy](https://realhunt.co/costs/italy) | Optional flat 'cedolare secca' on short lets: 21% for one property, 26% from the second. | Every tourist let needs a national CIN code shown on listings and at the property; from the 3rd property it is treated as a business (VAT registration).
[Japan](https://realhunt.co/costs/japan) | Rent paid to a non-resident is subject to 20.42% withholding (except when an individual rents it as their own home), and the owner must file a tax return each year through a tax representative in Japan to settle the final tax. | No sourced summary
[Lombok](https://realhunt.co/costs/lombok) | Non-residents: 20% withholding on gross rent (10% possible under a treaty); PT PMA 22% corporate tax. | Pondok Wisata licence required for short-term rental; foreigners must operate through a PT PMA.
[Mexico](https://realhunt.co/costs/mexico) | Non-residents: 25% ISR withholding on gross rent; plus 16% IVA on short-term stays (Airbnb remits on its bookings). | Quintana Roo: mandatory RETUR-Q registration (since Aug 2025, renewed annually) plus a state operating licence and RFC tax ID; 6% lodging tax; fines up to MXN 100,000.
[Montenegro](https://realhunt.co/costs/montenegro) | Around 15% withholding for non-residents. | Short-term rentals must be registered and pay a municipal tourist tax per guest-night.
[Netherlands](https://realhunt.co/costs/netherlands) | Non-residents declare Dutch property in box 3, where tax is 36% on a deemed return of 6% of the property's value in 2026, after a tax-free allowance of EUR 59,357 per person, regardless of actual rent. | No sourced summary
[Northern Cyprus](https://realhunt.co/costs/northern-cyprus) | 10% of gross rental income (Investra, 2026). | Must register with the Ministry of Tourism and hold a licence for short-term letting; monthly tax reporting.
[Norway](https://realhunt.co/costs/norway) | Rental profit is normally taxed at 22%, and the Tax Administration says its rental rules also apply to owners who are tax resident abroad. | No sourced summary
[Poland](https://realhunt.co/costs/poland) | Private rental income is taxed as a flat lump sum (ryczałt) of 8.5% of revenue up to PLN 100,000 a year and 12.5% above that. | No sourced summary
[Portugal](https://realhunt.co/costs/portugal) | Long-term: 25% flat for non-residents; short-term (AL) under the simplified regime only 35-50% of gross is taxable. | Alojamento Local (AL) registration is mandatory; since Nov 2024 municipalities can freeze new AL licences in containment zones (Lisbon, Porto use this); condominiums can object with >50% of owners.
[Spain](https://realhunt.co/costs/spain) | Non-residents: EU/EEA 19% on net income; non-EU 24% on gross with no deductions. | Regional tourist licence plus the national single rental registry number (mandatory since 1 Jul 2025); new tourist lets in apartment blocks need 3/5 owners' approval (since 3 Apr 2025).
[Sweden](https://realhunt.co/costs/sweden) | Non-resident individuals pay 30% tax on net rental income as capital income; for a private home you can first deduct SEK 40,000 per property and 20% of the rent (the 20% does not apply to a bostadsrätt). | No sourced summary
[Switzerland](https://realhunt.co/costs/switzerland) | Non-residents pay tax on net Swiss rental income at ordinary cantonal and communal rates plus federal direct tax, and some cantons set the rate using worldwide income. | No sourced summary
[United Kingdom](https://realhunt.co/costs/united-kingdom) | Non-resident landlords pay UK income tax on rent at 20%, 40% or 45%, with 20% deducted at source by the agent or tenant unless HMRC approves gross payment, and the rates on property income are set to rise to 22%, 42% and 47% from April 2027. | No sourced summary
[United States](https://realhunt.co/costs/united-states) | By default a non-resident pays 30% of gross rent (or a lower treaty rate), withheld at source, or can elect to treat the rent as business income and pay graduated rates on net income by filing Form 1040-NR and giving Form W-8ECI to the withholding agent. | No sourced summary
[Vietnam](https://realhunt.co/costs/vietnam) | 10% of gross rent (5% VAT + 5% PIT) above the exemption threshold; threshold raised to VND 1 billion/yr from 1 Jan 2026 (older guides say VND 100 million). | Guests must be registered with local police; HCMC (Decision 19/2026, from 25 Apr 2026) allows apartment short-lets only as registered, licensed accommodation providers; frequent/multi-unit renting needs a business registration.

### Someone has to be there

Rent also brings paperwork in the country of the house. In the United States a foreign owner chooses between 30% tax on the gross rent and a net-income election that needs a yearly tax return. In Germany a non-resident landlord deals with a German tax office. In Japan a non-resident owner needs a tax representative with a Japanese address. We have no sourced figures for what a manager or a key holder charges, so we give none: ask for the fee as a share of rent and for what it does not include.

## Spain's wealth tax for owners who live abroad: from what amount it applies

A non-resident owner pays Spanish wealth tax only on the assets located in Spain, and the first €700,000 is exempt. Someone whose only Spanish asset is a house worth less than that owes nothing under the state rule.

Reviewed on 14 November 2026 · Rules and figures as of November 2026 · General information, not legal or tax advice

### What the tax agency says

People who live in Spain are taxed on their worldwide net wealth, wherever the assets are. Non-residents are taxed under what the agency calls the obligación real: only on the assets and rights located in Spain. To work out the net amount, only the charges on those Spanish assets, and debts for money invested in them, can be deducted: a mortgage on the Spanish house counts, a loan on your home elsewhere does not.

There is an exempt minimum of €700,000 for non-residents taxed this way. The tax is counted on what you own on 31 December of each year: there is no tax period, only that date.

Source: [Agencia Tributaria](https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/no-residentes/impuesto-sobre-patrimonio/exigibilidad-impuesto-sobre-patrimonio-no-residentes.html)

### What it means for the homes on RealHunt

We list cheap homes, so the arithmetic is short.

Today RealHunt lists 191 homes in Spain. Their median asking price is €97,000 and the most expensive costs €348,000, which is 50% of the €700,000 exempt minimum. A non-resident whose only asset in Spain is one of these homes is below the threshold of the state rule.

[All 191 homes in Spain](https://realhunt.co/homes/spain)

### What this page does not cover

The regions of Spain can change the wealth tax, and this page only states the state rule we read on the tax agency's page; we have not sourced the regional differences, so we do not list them. Wealth tax is also not the yearly cost that actually reaches a small owner: a non-resident who keeps a house for their own use declares imputed income on it every year, and pays the council's IBI. See [first-year costs](https://realhunt.co/guide/buying/first-year-costs) and the [Spain glossary](https://realhunt.co/guide/glossary/spain).

Sources: [Agencia Tributaria](https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/no-residentes/impuesto-sobre-patrimonio/exigibilidad-impuesto-sobre-patrimonio-no-residentes.html) · [Agencia Tributaria](https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/no-residentes/irnr-sin-establecimiento-permanente/cuestiones-especificas-sobre-tributacion-inmuebles.html)

Buying guide

## Tax residency and the 183-day rule: how four countries really count

Owning a house does not make you a tax resident; living in it for long enough can. There is no single 183-day rule: Spain counts more than 183 days in the calendar year and also looks at where your economic interests are, the United Kingdom has several tests, the United States adds up three years and Germany looks at a continuous stay of more than six months.

Reviewed on 14 November 2026 · Rules and figures as of November 2026 · General information, not legal or tax advice

### Spain

The Spanish tax agency treats a person as resident when either of two things is true: they stay in Spain more than 183 days during the calendar year, or the main core of their activities or economic interests is in Spain, directly or indirectly. Sporadic absences are counted as days in Spain unless the person proves tax residence in another country.

Example: you spend 1 April to 30 September in your house in Granada, 183 days. That is not more than 183. Add a ten-day visit at Christmas and you are at 193: resident by the day count, with your worldwide income in the Spanish return.

Source: [Agencia Tributaria](https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/no-residentes/residencia-personas-fisicas-juridicas/persona-fisica-residente-espana.html)

### United Kingdom

The UK uses a set of tests. You may be resident under the automatic UK tests if you spent 183 or more days in the UK in the tax year. You are usually non-resident if you spent fewer than 16 days in the UK, or fewer than 46 if you were not UK resident in the three previous tax years. Between those lines, the number of days is weighed against your ties to the UK, such as work or family.

Example: a British couple who move to their house in France and return for three weeks a year stay well under 46 days, but a home and work kept in the UK change the answer. The day count alone is not the test.

Source: [GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/tax-foreign-income/residence)

### United States

For someone who is not a US citizen, the substantial presence test asks for at least 31 days in the current year and 183 days over three years, counting every day of the current year, one third of the days of the year before and one sixth of the days of the year before that. The tax agency's own example: 120 days in each of three years gives 120 + 40 + 20 = 180, so the person is not resident under the test.

For US citizens none of this matters: they are taxed on worldwide income wherever they live. See [Americans buying abroad](https://realhunt.co/guide/buying/americans-buying-abroad).

Sources: [Internal Revenue Service](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/substantial-presence-test) · [Internal Revenue Service](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/us-citizens-and-resident-aliens-abroad)

### Germany

The Fiscal Code speaks of habitual abode rather than of 183 days: a continuous stay of more than six months always counts as habitual abode from its first day, and short interruptions are ignored. A stay only for a visit, a holiday, a cure or similar private purposes that lasts no more than a year is left out.

Source: [Bundesministerium der Justiz](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/ao_1977/__9.html)

### What the house itself triggers

A home abroad brings tax in the country where it stands even if you never become resident there. In Spain a non-resident owner declares imputed income on a home kept for their own use or left empty, rental income if it is let and the gain when it is sold. In the Netherlands non-residents pay box 3 income tax on the value of the property. In Japan a non-resident owner must name a tax representative. More in [Do I pay tax in my own country too?](https://realhunt.co/guide/questions/do-i-pay-tax-at-home-too).

Sources: [Agencia Tributaria](https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/no-residentes/irnr-sin-establecimiento-permanente/cuestiones-especificas-sobre-tributacion-inmuebles.html) · [RealHunt country file: Netherlands](https://realhunt.co/costs/netherlands) · [RealHunt country file: Japan](https://realhunt.co/costs/japan)

Buying guide

## Living in the house you bought: residency, registration and health cover

No: in almost every country in our files, buying a home gives no right to live there, and the property routes that existed in Spain and Portugal have closed. EU citizens can live in another EU country anyway and register after three months. Everyone else needs a visa based on income, work or family, not on the house.

Reviewed on 14 November 2026 · Rules and figures as of November 2026 · General information, not legal or tax advice

### What each country says to buyers from outside the EU

From our own file of rules by nationality. A cheap home never reaches the thresholds of the few investment routes that remain.

Bulgaria
Buying a home gives no right to live in Bulgaria; longer stays need a residence permit.

Canada
Buying a home gives no right to live in Canada.

Cyprus
Non-EU buyers of a new home worth at least €300,000 plus VAT can apply for permanent residency under the Cyprus investment route; the conditions were tightened in 2023, so check the current rules.

Denmark
Buying a home gives no right to live in Denmark.

Dominican Republic
Buying a home does not by itself give you residency in the Dominican Republic.

France
Buying a home gives no right to live in France; stays over 90 days need a long-stay visa.

Germany
Buying a home gives no right to live in Germany.

Greece
Greece has a golden visa for non-EU buyers. Since 2024 the minimum is €800,000 in Attica, Thessaloniki, Mykonos, Santorini and larger islands, and €400,000 elsewhere, so a cheap home does not qualify.

Italy
Buying a home gives no right to live in Italy; stays over 90 days need a visa, such as the elective residence visa.

Japan
Buying a home gives no visa or residency in Japan.

Mexico
Buying a home gives no residency in Mexico; temporary residency is usually based on income or savings and applied for at a Mexican consulate.

Netherlands
Buying a home gives no right to live in the Netherlands.

Norway
Buying a home gives no right to live in Norway.

Poland
Buying a home gives no right to live in Poland.

Portugal
Since October 2023, buying a home no longer qualifies for Portugal's golden visa. The D7 visa for people with passive income is the usual route to live there.

Spain
Buying a home gives no right to live in Spain: the golden visa for property buyers closed on 3 April 2025. The non-lucrative visa is the usual route for people with passive income.

Sweden
Buying a home gives no right to live in Sweden.

Switzerland
Buying a home gives no right to live in Switzerland.

United Kingdom
Buying a home gives no right to live in the UK. Visitors can usually stay up to 6 months, and most now need an electronic travel authorisation (ETA) before they travel.

United States
Buying a home gives no visa or right to live in the US; visits follow the normal visitor rules for your passport.

Source: [RealHunt rules by nationality](https://realhunt.co/can-i-buy)

### EU citizens: registering after three months

An EU citizen has the right to live in another EU country, with or without a house. The EU's guide says that after three months in the new country you may be required to register your residence with the relevant authority, often the town hall or the local police station, and that you then receive a registration certificate, which should be issued immediately and cost no more than nationals pay for an identity card.

If you are required to register and do not, you may be fined, but you can go on living in the country and cannot be expelled just for that.

Source: [Your Europe (European Union)](https://europa.eu/youreurope/citizens/residence/documents-formalities/registering-residence/index_en.htm)

### Visitors from outside the EU: 90 days in every 180

Without a visa, the usual limit in the Schengen area is 90 days in every 180, counted across all its countries together. The British government's guidance spells it out for its citizens and it makes no exception for owners. Two long stays a year in your own house fit; living there does not. See [British buyers after Brexit](https://realhunt.co/guide/buying/british-buyers-after-brexit).

Sources: [GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/travel-to-eu-schengen-area) · [RealHunt rules by nationality](https://realhunt.co/can-i-buy)

### Health cover while you are there

Owning a house gives no health cover. For temporary stays, people insured in an EU country use the European Health Insurance Card, which is free from your own health insurer and is the proof that you are insured. It gives access to public healthcare on the same conditions as people insured in that country. It does not cover private healthcare or treatment you travel for on purpose.

We have not sourced the rules for people who move for good or for visitors from outside the EU, so this page stops here: ask the health service of the country, and count private insurance into your budget until you have an answer.

Source: [Your Europe (European Union)](https://europa.eu/youreurope/citizens/health/unplanned-healthcare/temporary-stays/index_en.htm)

## How to buy a home in Canada as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Mostly not for now: a federal ban stops non-Canadians from buying homes in cities and larger towns until January 1, 2027, with exceptions such as work permit holders and spouses of citizens or permanent residents. The ban does not cover rural areas and small towns, and the government has said it does not plan simply to extend it, but a replacement is being studied.

### The steps

- Check if you can buy: Until January 1, 2027, non-Canadians cannot buy homes in census metropolitan areas or census agglomerations unless an exception applies. Check the location and your status first.
- Check provincial foreign buyer taxes: Ontario charges foreign buyers 25% and British Columbia charges 20% in some regions. These taxes can cost more than the rest of the purchase costs combined.
- Hire a real estate lawyer: The lawyer checks the title, handles the funds and registers the transfer. Ask for a written fee estimate first.
- Make an offer: Sign a purchase agreement with your price and conditions, such as a home inspection.
- Close the sale: On closing day you pay the balance plus land transfer tax and fees through your lawyer, and the home is registered in your name.
- Arrange rental tax filings: If you rent it out, name a Canadian agent to withhold tax, consider filing Form NR6, and file a Section 216 return each year.

### Costs on top of the price

About 1.5-4%: Buyers usually pay provincial land transfer tax on a sliding scale (Ontario: 0.5% up to $55,000 and 1% from $55,000 to $250,000), legal fees of about $500 to $1,500, title insurance of about $250 and an inspection of $300 to $1,000, while the seller usually pays the agents; foreign buyers also pay Ontario's 25% non-resident speculation tax anywhere in Ontario and British Columbia's 20% additional tax in Metro Vancouver and four other regions.

### Every year

Expect municipal property tax, from about 0.3% to 2.1% of assessed value depending on the city, plus insurance and upkeep. The federal Underused Housing Tax is proposed to end from 2025, but the change was still in Bill C-15 when last checked.

Yearly property tax: Property tax is set by each city as a share of assessed value, from about 0.3% in Vancouver to 2.12% in Saint John in 2026.

Tax on rental income: Non-residents have 25% of gross rent withheld, but they can file a Section 216 return to pay tax on net rent instead, and Form NR6 lets the agent withhold on net rent.

## How to buy a home in Cyprus as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

EU citizens buy without restrictions. Non-EU buyers need permission from the Council of Ministers, applied for through the District Officer, and are normally limited to one home or a plot of up to 4,014 m².

### The steps

- Hire a lawyer: Use a Cyprus lawyer to negotiate and draft the sale contract and run the checks.
- Check the title: The lawyer searches the District Land Registry for ownership, mortgages, court claims and restrictions, and checks permits and VAT status.
- Sign the contract: Sign the sale agreement with the price and payment terms. It is legally binding once signed.
- Lodge the contract: Deposit the signed contract at the Land Registry under the Specific Performance Law to protect your right to the title.
- Apply for permission if non-EU: Non-EU buyers apply to the Council of Ministers through the District Officer, usually after signing. The title cannot be registered without it.
- Transfer the title: Pay the balance and transfer fees, then transfer the title deed at the District Land Registry.

### Costs on top of the price

About 2.5-3.5%: Land Registry transfer fees of 3% up to €85,000, 5% to €170,000 and 8% above, halved for resales without VAT (1.5%, 2.5% and 4%); stamp duty abolished from 1 January 2026; lawyer about 1% plus VAT; small Land Registry charges.

### Every year

Yearly costs are municipal, sewerage and local authority fees, plus income tax and GHS on any rent.

Yearly property tax: There is no annual national property tax (abolished in 2017); owners pay municipal fees of about €90 to €300 a year, plus sewerage and local authority charges.

Tax on rental income: Non-residents pay income tax on Cyprus rental income at 20% to 35% after deducting 20% of the gross rent and loan interest, plus a 2.65% health contribution (GHS); the special defence contribution does not apply to them.

## How to buy a home in Denmark as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Without Danish domicile or 5 years of past residence you need permission from the Department of Civil Affairs (Civilstyrelsen); EU/EEA citizens who live and are registered in Denmark can buy a permanent home without permission by signing a declaration to the Land Registration Court. Holiday homes (sommerhuse) need permission, which is only given to people with particularly strong ties to Denmark, such as many years of holidays there.

### The steps

- Check if you need permission: Use Civilstyrelsen's rules: EU/EEA citizens living in Denmark sign a declaration, everyone else applies for permission for the specific property.
- Get a Danish tax number: If you have no Danish personal number, request one from the Danish Tax Agency with form 04.063_AP_EN.
- Set a budget with a bank: Danish banks usually lend up to 80% of the value, so plan for at least a 20% down payment.
- Make an offer and sign with conditions: The seller's agent drafts the contract; have your own lawyer review it and add bank and lawyer approval clauses (bank- og advokatforbehold).
- Let your lawyer check the documents: Your lawyer reviews the condition report, title and registered charges before the clauses are lifted.
- Register the deed: The deed (skøde) is registered digitally with the Land Registration Court and the registration fee is paid, which makes you the legal owner.

### Costs on top of the price

About 1.5-3%: Registration fee on the deed (tinglysningsafgift) of DKK 1,850 plus 0.6% of the price, about 1% for a buyer's lawyer, and, if you borrow, a mortgage registration fee of DKK 1,825 plus 1.25% of the loan; the seller normally pays the agent.

### Every year

Expect property value tax and municipal land tax, both charged through the Danish tax system, plus insurance, utilities and upkeep. Owners abroad may need to file a Danish tax return if they rent the home out.

Yearly property tax: Owners pay property value tax (ejendomsværdiskat) of 0.51% on 80% of the official valuation (1.4% above DKK 9.2 million) plus municipal land tax (grundskyld) at a rate set by each municipality, capped at 30 per mille of the land value.

Tax on rental income: A non-resident who rents out a Danish home is taxed in Denmark on the profit under the ordinary Danish rules; staying in Denmark more than 3 months at a time or 180 days a year, or working there, makes you fully tax liable.

## How to buy a home in the Dominican Republic as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Yes. Foreigners have the same rights as Dominican citizens to buy land and homes, with no restrictions.

### The steps

- Get a tax ID (RNC): Get your RNC at a DGII office with your passport, or through a lawyer with a notarized power of attorney. You need it to sign and to register the title.
- Check the title: Have a Dominican lawyer confirm a clean title at the Title Registry, with no liens or lawsuits, and that IPI tax, utilities and condo fees are paid.
- Sign a promise of sale: Sign the promise of sale contract and pay a deposit, usually 10-20%. It usually sets a 30 to 60 day window to complete.
- Sign the deed before a notary: Pay the balance and sign the deed of sale. The notary legalizes the document.
- Pay the transfer tax: Pay the 3% transfer tax to DGII. The title cannot be registered until it is paid.
- Register the title: Your lawyer files the deed and tax receipt at the Title Registry. The new title certificate in your name usually takes 30 to 90 days.

### Costs on top of the price

About 4.25-7%: The buyer pays a 3% transfer tax (0% for qualifying first purchases under CONFOTUR tourism incentives), legal fees of about 1-2% and notary fees of about 0.25-1%, plus registration costs, while the seller pays the 2-3% agent fee.

### Every year

Most single homes under about $150,000 pay no IPI property tax because they fall under the threshold, but expect condo fees, utilities and upkeep. A 2026 tax law (Law 30-26) sets a 10% tax on gains when an individual sells, though its regulations were still in draft in October 2026.

Yearly property tax: The yearly IPI tax is 1% of the part of a person's total Dominican property value, as assessed by the tax office DGII, above RD$10,695,494 in 2026, so a single cheap home is often below the threshold.

Tax on rental income: Rent paid abroad to a non-resident is generally subject to 27% withholding.
