## Can an Australian buy property in Sweden?

Short answer: Yes.

Yes. There are no citizenship or residence rules for buying a home in Sweden. You need a Swedish personal identity number or a coordination number (samordningsnummer) to register ownership.

General information, not legal advice. Updated November 2026.

### What it costs to buy

About 1.5-3.5% on top of the price. On a €150,000 home that is €2,250 to €5,250, so €152,250 to €155,250 in total.

Stamp duty on the title (lagfart) of 1.5% of the price or tax value, whichever is higher, plus a SEK 825 fee; if you borrow and need new mortgage deeds (pantbrev), 2% of their amount plus a SEK 375 fee; optional legal advice; the seller normally pays the agent, and a cooperative flat (bostadsrätt) has no lagfart.

[Work it out for your price](https://realhunt.co/buying-costs/sweden)

### Every year

Yearly property tax: Houses pay a municipal property fee (kommunal fastighetsavgift) of SEK 10,425 in 2026, or 0.75% of the tax value if that is lower.

House owners pay the municipal property fee and must file a Swedish tax return if they owe it or have rental income, even when living abroad. Add insurance, utilities and upkeep.

Tax on rental income: Non-resident individuals pay 30% tax on net rental income as capital income; for a private home you can first deduct SEK 40,000 per property and 20% of the rent (the 20% does not apply to a bostadsrätt).

### Living there

Buying a home gives no right to live in Sweden.

Sweden is in the Schengen area: with an Australian passport you can usually stay up to 90 days in any 180 days across the whole area without a visa.

### Good to know as an Australian

- Australian tax residents are taxed on worldwide income, so rent from a home abroad goes on your Australian return, usually with a credit for tax paid abroad.

### The steps to buy in Sweden

- Get a coordination number
- Open a Swedish bank account
- Find a home and arrange money
- Inspect before you commit
- Sign the purchase contract
- Apply for title at Lantmäteriet

[The full guide, step by step](https://realhunt.co/guide/sweden)

## Can an Australian buy property in Switzerland?

Short answer: Restricted.

Restricted. Under the Lex Koller law, Australians living abroad need a cantonal permit and can usually only buy one holiday home in a tourist area, within national quotas. Living in Switzerland, holders of a C permit buy like Swiss citizens, and holders of a B permit can buy the home they live in.

General information, not legal advice. Updated November 2026.

### What it costs to buy

About 1-5% on top of the price. On a €150,000 home that is €1,500 to €7,500, so €151,500 to €157,500 in total.

Transfer tax (Handänderungssteuer, droits de mutation) 0% to about 3.3% depending on the canton; notary about 0.1-0.5%; land register fee, a small fixed amount or percentage; optional lawyer 1-2%; the agent fee (2-3%) is paid by the seller.

[Work it out for your price](https://realhunt.co/buying-costs/switzerland)

### Every year

Yearly property tax: More than half of the cantons charge an annual property tax (Liegenschaftssteuer), usually 0.01-0.3% of the assessed value, and owners also pay cantonal wealth tax on the property value minus the mortgage.

Yearly costs are wealth tax, cantonal property tax where it exists, and tax on imputed rental value (Eigenmietwert) if you use the home yourself. Imputed rental value is due to end on 1 January 2029, and cantons may then add a new tax on second homes.

Tax on rental income: Non-residents pay tax on net Swiss rental income at ordinary cantonal and communal rates plus federal direct tax, and some cantons set the rate using worldwide income.

### Living there

Buying a home gives no right to live in Switzerland.

Switzerland is in the Schengen area: with an Australian passport you can usually stay up to 90 days in any 180 days across the whole area without a visa.

### Good to know as an Australian

- Australian tax residents are taxed on worldwide income, so rent from a home abroad goes on your Australian return, usually with a credit for tax paid abroad.

### The steps to buy in Switzerland

- Check your Lex Koller status
- Arrange financing
- Find a property and make an offer
- Sign the deed at a notary
- Register the transfer

[The full guide, step by step](https://realhunt.co/guide/switzerland)

## Can a British citizen buy property in Norway?

Short answer: Yes.

Yes. Anyone with the funds can buy property in Norway, and a built plot of up to 2 decares normally needs no concession (konsesjon). Farms and larger plots need a concession.

General information, not legal advice. Updated November 2026.

### What it costs to buy

About 2.5-3% on top of the price. On a €150,000 home that is €3,750 to €4,500, so €153,750 to €154,500 in total.

Document duty (dokumentavgift) of 2.5% of market value, a registration fee (tinglysingsgebyr) of NOK 545 for the deed and NOK 545 for any mortgage document; a flat in a housing cooperative (borettslag) has no document duty; the seller normally pays the agent.

[Work it out for your price](https://realhunt.co/buying-costs/norway)

### Every year

Yearly property tax: Some municipalities charge property tax (eiendomsskatt), at most 4 per mille of the value after a reduction of at least 30%, and some also give a basic deduction; many charge nothing.

Expect municipal property tax where it applies, municipal fees, insurance and upkeep. Costs such as municipal fees and property tax are deductible against rental income.

Tax on rental income: Rental profit is normally taxed at 22%, and the Tax Administration says its rental rules also apply to owners who are tax resident abroad.

### Living there

Buying a home gives no right to live in Norway.

Norway is in the Schengen area: with a British passport you can usually stay up to 90 days in any 180 days across the whole area without a visa.

### Good to know as a British citizen

- Since Brexit, British buyers count as non-EU buyers, so the non-EU rules and tax rates apply (for example on rental income).

### The steps to buy in Norway

- Find a home and get loan approval
- Bid through the agent
- Sign the contract
- Pay at settlement
- Get a D-number if needed
- Register the deed

[The full guide, step by step](https://realhunt.co/guide/norway)

### Questions

#### Can a British citizen buy property in Norway?

Yes. Anyone with the funds can buy property in Norway, and a built plot of up to 2 decares normally needs no concession (konsesjon). Farms and larger plots need a concession.

#### How much are the buying costs in Norway?

About 2.5-3% on top of the price, so €3,750 to €4,500 on a €150,000 home. Document duty (dokumentavgift) of 2.5% of market value, a registration fee (tinglysingsgebyr) of NOK 545 for the deed and NOK 545 for any mortgage document; a flat in a housing cooperative (borettslag) has no document duty; the seller normally pays the agent.

#### Is there a yearly property tax in Norway?

Some municipalities charge property tax (eiendomsskatt), at most 4 per mille of the value after a reduction of at least 30%, and some also give a basic deduction; many charge nothing.

#### What tax do I pay on rent in Norway if I live abroad?

Rental profit is normally taxed at 22%, and the Tax Administration says its rental rules also apply to owners who are tax resident abroad.

#### Does buying a home in Norway let me live there as a British citizen?

Buying a home gives no right to live in Norway. Norway is in the Schengen area: with a British passport you can usually stay up to 90 days in any 180 days across the whole area without a visa.

### Buying costs and rules for foreigners in Italy

Can foreigners buy? Yes for EU citizens; non-EU buyers need reciprocity (US, UK, Canada, Australia qualify).

Taxes and fees add about 4 to 15% to the price: Registration tax 9% on a second home (resale), or VAT on new builds; notary 1-2% + legal ~1% + agent ~3% (GPG roundtrip 10-18%). On the median home on this page (€30,000) that is €1,200 to €4,500, so €31,200 to €34,500 in all.

To keep the whole purchase within €100,000, look at asking prices up to about €86,900: 10 of these 11 homes fit.

### Buying costs and rules for foreigners in Spain

Can foreigners buy? Yes, no restrictions at present; the government has proposed a 100% tax on (or ban for) non-EU non-resident buyers, not enacted.

Taxes and fees add about 7.5 to 14% to the price: New build: 10% IVA + 0.5-1.5% AJD stamp duty + notary 0.5-1% + legal 1-2%; resale: ITP transfer tax 6-11% instead of IVA/AJD. On the median home on this page (€91,000) that is €6,825 to €12,740, so €97,825 to €103,740 in all.

To keep the whole purchase within €100,000, look at asking prices up to about €87,700: 11 of these 27 homes fit.

### Buying costs and rules for foreigners in Sweden

Can foreigners buy? Yes. There are no citizenship or residence rules for buying a home in Sweden, but you need a Swedish personal identity number or coordination number (samordningsnummer) to register ownership.

Taxes and fees add about 1.5 to 3.5% to the price: Stamp duty on the title (lagfart) of 1.5% of the price or tax value, whichever is higher, plus a SEK 825 fee; if you borrow and need new mortgage deeds (pantbrev), 2% of their amount plus a SEK 375 fee; optional legal advice; the seller normally pays the agent, and a cooperative flat (bostadsrätt) has no lagfart. On the median home on this page (€98,100) that is €1,472 to €3,434, so €99,572 to €101,534 in all.

To keep the whole purchase within €100,000, look at asking prices up to about €96,600: 2 of these 4 homes fit.

### Buying costs and rules for foreigners in Italy

Can foreigners buy? Yes for EU citizens; non-EU buyers need reciprocity (US, UK, Canada, Australia qualify).

Taxes and fees add about 4 to 15% to the price: Registration tax 9% on a second home (resale), or VAT on new builds; notary 1-2% + legal ~1% + agent ~3% (GPG roundtrip 10-18%). On the median home on this page (€29,000) that is €1,160 to €4,350, so €30,160 to €33,350 in all.

To keep the whole purchase within €50,000, look at asking prices up to about €43,400: 7 of these 9 homes fit.

### Buying costs and rules for foreigners in Canada

Can foreigners buy? Mostly not for now: a federal ban stops non-Canadians from buying homes in cities and larger towns until January 1, 2027, with exceptions such as work permit holders and spouses of citizens or permanent residents. The ban does not cover rural areas and small towns, and the government has said it does not plan simply to extend it, but a replacement is being studied.

Taxes and fees add about 1.5 to 4% to the price: Buyers usually pay provincial land transfer tax on a sliding scale (Ontario: 0.5% up to $55,000 and 1% from $55,000 to $250,000), legal fees of about $500 to $1,500, title insurance of about $250 and an inspection of $300 to $1,000, while the seller usually pays the agents; foreign buyers also pay Ontario's 25% non-resident speculation tax anywhere in Ontario and British Columbia's 20% additional tax in Metro Vancouver and four other regions. On the median home on this page (€99,500) that is €1,493 to €3,980, so €100,993 to €103,480 in all.

### Buying costs and rules for foreigners in Denmark

Can foreigners buy? Without Danish domicile or 5 years of past residence you need permission from the Department of Civil Affairs (Civilstyrelsen); EU/EEA citizens who live and are registered in Denmark can buy a permanent home without permission by signing a declaration to the Land Registration Court. Holiday homes (sommerhuse) need permission, which is only given to people with particularly strong ties to Denmark, such as many years of holidays there.

Taxes and fees add about 1.5 to 3% to the price: Registration fee on the deed (tinglysningsafgift) of DKK 1,850 plus 0.6% of the price, about 1% for a buyer's lawyer, and, if you borrow, a mortgage registration fee of DKK 1,825 plus 1.25% of the loan; the seller normally pays the agent. On the median home on this page (€90,500) that is €1,358 to €2,715, so €91,858 to €93,215 in all.

### Buying costs and rules for foreigners in France

Can foreigners buy? Yes. Foreigners can buy property in France without major restrictions, and non-EU buyers do not need a permit, although the paperwork can take longer.

Taxes and fees add about 7 to 8.5% to the price: Transfer taxes (droits de mutation) of about 5.8%, or about 6.3% in departments that raised their rate for 2025 to March 2028; notary fee (émoluments) on a sliding scale from 3.87% down to 0.799% plus 20% VAT, about 1.3% on a €150,000 home; land security contribution (contribution de sécurité immobilière) 0.10%; disbursements (débours) of about €800 to €1,200; the agent fee is usually built into the advertised price (FAI) and paid by the seller, sometimes shared. On the median home on this page (€136,250) that is €9,538 to €11,581, so €145,788 to €147,831 in all.

### Buying costs and rules for foreigners in Germany

Can foreigners buy? Yes. There are no restrictions on foreigners buying property in Germany, though non-EU buyers usually need a bigger down payment to get a loan.

Taxes and fees add about 5 to 8.5% to the price: Real estate transfer tax (Grunderwerbsteuer) of 3.5% to 6.5% depending on the state (3.5% in Bavaria, 6.5% in Brandenburg, North Rhine-Westphalia, Saarland and Schleswig-Holstein), plus notary and land registry fees (Notar- und Grundbuchkosten) of about 1.5-2%; if the seller hired the agent, the buyer pays half the commission by law, which is extra. On the median home on this page (€50,000) that is €2,500 to €4,250, so €52,500 to €54,250 in all.

### Buying costs and rules for foreigners in Greece

Can foreigners buy? Yes. Buyers from outside the EU and EFTA need a permit to buy in designated border areas (parts of northern Greece and eastern Aegean islands such as the Dodecanese and Rhodes). The government has announced a 15% transfer tax for non-EU buyers of homes from 1 January 2027, not yet final in September 2026.

Taxes and fees add about 5.5 to 7% to the price: Transfer tax 3.09% of the price or the taxable value, whichever is higher; notary about 0.8-1% plus VAT; land registry fees about 0.5-0.7%; lawyer 1-2% plus VAT; if an agent is used, the buyer usually pays a commission of 1-3% plus VAT on top. On the median home on this page (€109,000) that is €5,995 to €7,630, so €114,995 to €116,630 in all.

### Buying costs and rules for foreigners in Italy

Can foreigners buy? Yes for EU citizens; non-EU buyers need reciprocity (US, UK, Canada, Australia qualify).

Taxes and fees add about 4 to 15% to the price: Registration tax 9% on a second home (resale), or VAT on new builds; notary 1-2% + legal ~1% + agent ~3% (GPG roundtrip 10-18%). On the median home on this page (€30,000) that is €1,200 to €4,500, so €31,200 to €34,500 in all.

### Buying costs and rules for foreigners in the Netherlands

Can foreigners buy? Yes. There are no nationality or residence rules and no surcharge for foreign buyers. Some cities, such as The Hague, restrict renting out cheaper homes after purchase without a permit (opkoopbescherming).

Taxes and fees add about 2 to 9% to the price: Transfer tax (overdrachtsbelasting) of 8% if you will not live in the home, such as a buy-to-let or holiday home, or 2% if it becomes your main home; a notary fee for the transfer deed of around EUR 500; Kadaster registration fees; and mortgage costs if you borrow; the seller pays its own agent. On the median home on this page (€315,000) that is €6,300 to €28,350, so €321,300 to €343,350 in all.

### Buying costs and rules for foreigners in Poland

Can foreigners buy? EU, EEA and Swiss citizens buy on the same terms as Poles. Other foreigners can buy an apartment without a permit, but usually need a permit from the Ministry of the Interior (MSWiA) to buy a house or land.

Taxes and fees add about 2.5 to 4% to the price: Tax on civil law transactions (PCC) 2% of the value, paid by the buyer within 14 days of the deed; notary fee (taksa notarialna) capped at PLN 1,010 plus 0.4% of the value above PLN 60,000, plus 23% VAT; court fee of PLN 200 to enter ownership in the land register (plus PLN 100 for a new register); optional lawyer about 1%; the agent fee (about 2-3%) depends on the agreement. On the median home on this page (€68,316) that is €1,708 to €2,733, so €70,024 to €71,049 in all.

### Buying costs and rules for foreigners in Spain

Can foreigners buy? Yes, no restrictions at present; the government has proposed a 100% tax on (or ban for) non-EU non-resident buyers, not enacted.

Taxes and fees add about 7.5 to 14% to the price: New build: 10% IVA + 0.5-1.5% AJD stamp duty + notary 0.5-1% + legal 1-2%; resale: ITP transfer tax 6-11% instead of IVA/AJD. On the median home on this page (€91,000) that is €6,825 to €12,740, so €97,825 to €103,740 in all.

### Buying costs and rules for foreigners in Canada

Can foreigners buy? Mostly not for now: a federal ban stops non-Canadians from buying homes in cities and larger towns until January 1, 2027, with exceptions such as work permit holders and spouses of citizens or permanent residents. The ban does not cover rural areas and small towns, and the government has said it does not plan simply to extend it, but a replacement is being studied.

Taxes and fees add about 1.5 to 4% to the price: Buyers usually pay provincial land transfer tax on a sliding scale (Ontario: 0.5% up to $55,000 and 1% from $55,000 to $250,000), legal fees of about $500 to $1,500, title insurance of about $250 and an inspection of $300 to $1,000, while the seller usually pays the agents; foreign buyers also pay Ontario's 25% non-resident speculation tax anywhere in Ontario and British Columbia's 20% additional tax in Metro Vancouver and four other regions. On the median home on this page (€92,552) that is €1,388 to €3,702, so €93,940 to €96,254 in all.

To keep the whole purchase within €100,000, look at asking prices up to about €96,100: 3 of these 5 homes fit.
